opening.argument: Judge, the description pairs an offer of free video clips with an imperative to subscribe: “Get Free Video Clips For You! SUBSCRIBE NOW For Your Free Video” (DESCRIPTION_0001). That is a promise of free digital content tied to a viewer action. The same opening line directs viewers to an external chat-room site (DESCRIPTION_0001). The question is not whether the video asks for money; it is whether its free-content pitch is being used to solicit participation. On the wording supplied, it is.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense points to free chat rooms and the social footage, but neither addresses the separate subscribe-for-a-free-video pitch in the description (DESCRIPTION_0001). The absence of a payment or credential request does not erase that stated promise-action pairing. The footage shows people socializing (F0024); it does not establish what, if anything, a subscribing viewer receives.

citations.quote: SUBSCRIBE NOW For Your Free Video

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The description does say “SUBSCRIBE NOW For Your Free Video” (DESCRIPTION_0001), but it also immediately supplies video links (DESCRIPTION_0001). It does not say that subscribing unlocks a withheld reward, requires verification, or starts a claim process. The explicit destination is a free chat-room site (DESCRIPTION_0001). Reading an ordinary subscription prompt as a deceptive reward flow requires a condition and mechanism the evidence does not show.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the signals together. The description also repeats no-sign-up and free-chat phrases (DESCRIPTION_0002). These are multiple low-friction assurances surrounding a request for viewer action. Nor does the absence of a visible payment request settle what the promoted actions involve. The case for concern rests on those combined signals, not on inventing a charge.
